claim: SARS-CoV-2 has infected more than half a billion people and has killed more than 6.4 million by the end of 2022.
source: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the causative agent for Corona Virus Disease 19 (COVID-19) has infected more than half a billion people and has killed more than 6.4 million by the end of 2022.
evidence: This is a factual statement about COVID-19 statistics that represents established knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: Paxlovid targets the main protease (NSP5) of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Two specific SARS-CoV-2 targeting drugs and several monoclonal antibodies have recently been approved, such as Paxlovid targeting the main protease (NSP5) (Owen et al., 2021) and Remdesivir which targets viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Sheahan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owen et al., 2021.

claim: Remdesivir targets viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
source: Two specific SARS-CoV-2 targeting drugs and several monoclonal antibodies have recently been approved, such as Paxlovid targeting the main protease (NSP5) (Owen et al., 2021) and Remdesivir which targets viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Sheahan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sheahan et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded genomic RNA of ca. 30 kb.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded genomic RNA of ca. 30 kb (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: There is a 79.5% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV genome sequences.
source: There is a 79.5% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV genome sequences (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is considered a new type of human-infecting β-coronavirus.
source: The difference in their genomes provided new insights and SARS-CoV-2 is therefore considered a new type of human-infecting β-coronavirus (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 genome has 14 open reading frames (ORFs).
source: The SARS-CoV-2 genome has 14 open reading frames (ORFs)(Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: After cleavage, 16 mature proteins are produced from PP1a and PP1ab, known as nonstructural proteins 1–16 (NSP).
source: After cleavage, 16 mature proteins are produced from PP1a and PP1ab, known as nonstructural proteins 1–16 (NSP), and these proteins are responsible for generating the Replication-Transcription Complex (RTC).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Malone et al., 2022 in the preceding sentence.

claim: NSP14 and NSP16 are essential for viral RNA capping.
source: Among the non-structural proteins, both NSP14 and NSP16 are essential for viral RNA capping (Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2022.

claim: NSP13 uses its RNA/NTP triphosphatase (TPase) activity to hydrolyze 5'γ-phosphate of the nascent RNA chain (pppN-RNA), which results in the formation of the diphosphate 5'-ppN end in the ppN-RNA.
source: First, a bifunctional NSP13 (helicase) uses its RNA/NTP triphosphatase (TPase) activity to hydrolyze 5'γ-phosphate of the nascent RNA chain (pppN-RNA), which results in the formation of the diphosphate 5'-ppN end in the ppN-RNA (Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2022.

claim: Both NSP14 and NSP16 act as S-adenosyl-L-Methionine (SAM) dependent methyl transferases.
source: During this process, both NSP14 and NSP16 act as S-adenosyl-L-Methionine (SAM) dependent methyl transferases, and SAM acts as the methyl group donor resulting in the formation of the by-product SAH (Krafcikova et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krafcikova et al., 2020.

claim: NSP10 acts as an activator and stimulator of enzymatic activities of NSP14 and NSP16.
source: It is important to note that the proofreading 3'-to-5'exoribonuclease (ExoN) in NSP14 and the 2'-O-MTase in NSP16 require an essential cofactor, NSP10, that acts as an activator and stimulator of enzymatic activities (Bouvet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bouvet et al., 2014.

claim: NSP10 does not stimulate the N7-MTase activity of NSP14.
source: Although NSP10 does not stimulate the N7-MTase activity of NSP14, the ExoN activity of NSP14 relies on the stimulatory factor NSP10 (Riccio et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riccio et al., 2022.

claim: The ExoN activity of NSP14 relies on the stimulatory factor NSP10.
source: Although NSP10 does not stimulate the N7-MTase activity of NSP14, the ExoN activity of NSP14 relies on the stimulatory factor NSP10 (Riccio et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riccio et al., 2022.

claim: The N-terminal ExoN domain of NSP14 is responsible for viral RNA proofreading to maintain a low mutation rate and the integrity of the viral genome.
source: The N-terminal ExoN domain of NSP14 is responsible for viral RNA proofreading to maintain a low mutation rate and the integrity of the viral genome (Lin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2021.

claim: Failure of NSP10 to bind to NSP14 decreases the ExoN activity and thus leads to a significantly lower replication fidelity and high lethal mutagenesis.
source: Failure of NSP10 to bind to NSP14 decreases the ExoN activity and thus leads to a significantly lower replication fidelity and high lethal mutagenesis (Riccio et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riccio et al., 2022.

claim: The ExoN activity is responsible for regulating genome recombination in SARS-CoV-2.
source: In addition, the ExoN activity is also responsible for other viral replication processes such as regulating genome recombination in SARS-CoV-2 (16) and escape from the host immune response (Becares et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Becares et al., 2016.

claim: The ExoN activity is responsible for escape from the host immune response.
source: In addition, the ExoN activity is also responsible for other viral replication processes such as regulating genome recombination in SARS-CoV-2 (16) and escape from the host immune response (Becares et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Becares et al., 2016.

claim: RNA viruses including coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 have a higher mutation rate than DNA viruses.
source: RNA viruses including coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 have a higher mutation rate than DNA viruses (Sanjuán et al., 2010), although the rate in coronaviruses is attenuated compared to other RNA viruses due to the presence of the ExoN activity (Callaway, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanjuán et al., 2010.

claim: The mutation rate in coronaviruses is attenuated compared to other RNA viruses due to the presence of the ExoN activity.
source: RNA viruses including coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 have a higher mutation rate than DNA viruses (Sanjuán et al., 2010), although the rate in coronaviruses is attenuated compared to other RNA viruses due to the presence of the ExoN activity (Callaway, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Callaway, 2020.

claim: Mutations rates of 6.677x10–4 substitutions per site per year have recently been reported for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Mutations rates of 6.677x10–4 substitutions per site per year have recently been reported for SARS-CoV-2 (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: Two single-letter mutations per month per SARS-CoV-2 virus have been reported.
source: Others reported two single-letter mutations per month per SARS-CoV-2 virus (Callaway, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Callaway, 2020.

claim: Novel SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VoC) have emerged over the last 2 years, which display higher infectivity, cause more severe disease, and can escape the effects of vaccination.
source: The study of these variations through full genome sequencing has become an essential surveillance tool, as novel SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VoC) have emerged over the last 2 years, which display higher infectivity, cause more severe disease, and can escape the effects of vaccination (Harvey et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harvey et al., 2021.

claim: A comprehensive analysis of >13 million globally collected whole-genome sequences (WGS) of SARS-CoV-2 was carried out to identify all currently known variants in NSP10.
source: To further understand the role of NSP10, we carried out a comprehensive analysis of >13 million globally collected whole-genome sequences (WGS) of SARS-CoV-2 obtained from the Global Initiative Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) and compared it with the reference genome Wuhan/WIV04/2019 to identify all currently known variants in NSP10.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study and is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: T12I, T102I, and A104V in NSP10 have been identified as the three most frequent variants.
source: T12I, T102I, and A104V in NSP10 have been identified as the three most frequent variants and characterized using X-ray crystallography, biophysical assays, and enhanced sampling simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript, including Figure 2a and Table 1.

claim: NSP10 is significantly less prone to mutation compared to other proteins such as spike and NSP6.
source: In contrast to other proteins such as spike and NSP6, NSP10 is significantly less prone to mutation due to its crucial role in replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript, including Figure 6.

claim: After deleting the sequences with unknown residues in NSP10, 7,070,539 WGS were used for sequence alignment analysis in the first phase.
source: In the first phase (January 30, 2022), after deleting the sequences with unknown residues (see Materials and methods) in NSP10, 7,070,539 WGS were used for sequence alignment analysis.

source: This is in stark contrast to SARS-CoV-2 NSP1, for which 933 mutations have been identified in only 295,000 genome sequences (Mou et al., 2021).

claim: NSP10 protects viral RNA from being recognized by host immune responses by acting as a cofactor for methylation of the 5' end (capping).
source: The coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 protects its RNA from being recognized by host immune responses by methylation of its 5' end, also known as capping. This process is carried out by two enzymes, non-structural protein 16 (NSP16) containing 2'-O-methyltransferase and NSP14 through its N7 methyltransferase activity, which are essential for the replication of the viral genome as well as evading the host's innate immunity. NSP10 acts as a crucial cofactor and stimulator of NSP14 and NSP16.
